t:
(a) In General.—Section 6657 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 is amended—
        (1) by striking “If any check or money order in payment of any amount” and inserting “If any instrument in payment, by any commercially acceptable means, of any amount”, and 
        (2) by striking “such check” each place it appears and inserting “such instrument”.  
    (b) Effective Dates.—The amendments made by this section shall apply to instruments tendered after the date of the enactment of this Act.

fable.w: This section only amends the Internal Revenue Code's bad-check penalty provision so that it covers any payment instrument, and sets an effective date. No tempting reading really exists: there is no consultation, hearing, comment period, rulemaking, advisory body, or right to sue involving any party outside the federal government. Taxpayers tendering payment instruments are not participating in a federal decision.
fable.s: by striking “If any check or money order in payment of any amount” and inserting “If any instrument in payment, by any commercially acceptable means, of any amount”

qwen_block.w: This section amends the Internal Revenue Code to update terminology regarding payment instruments (changing 'check' to 'instrument'). It does not establish any process for public comment, consultation with outside entities, advisory boards, or hearings. The changes are purely technical and administrative, affecting how payments are defined, not how decisions are made with outside participation.
qwen_block.s: Section 6657 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 is amended— (1) by striking “If any check or money order in payment of any amount” and inserting “If any instrument in payment, by any commercially acceptable means, of any amount”, and (2) by striking “such check” each place it appears and inserting “such instrument”.

opus.w: This section is a technical amendment that widens the bad-check penalty to any payment instrument and sets an effective date. It requires no consultation, comment period, hearing, advisory body or right to sue. The fact that taxpayers pay with these instruments is not participation in a federal decision, so nothing here crosses the federal boundary.
opus.b:
1. **Reasoning.** The only tempting reading is that this section deals with the IRS and taxpayers, so outsiders might seem to be involved. That reading fails. The section only changes the wording of the bad-check penalty in IRC §6657 so that it covers any payment instrument, not just checks and money orders. It also sets an effective date. Nobody outside the federal government is consulted, and there is no comment period, hearing, advisory body or right to sue.

2. **Label.**

qwen_chat.w: This section amends the Internal Revenue Code to broaden the definition of acceptable payment instruments for tax liabilities. It does not establish any process for consultation, coordination, or input from outside parties (such as the public, states, or experts) before a federal decision is made. It is a substantive regulatory change, not a participatory mechanism.
qwen_chat.s: (a) In General.—Section 6657 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 is amended— (1) by striking “If any check or money order in payment of any amount” and inserting “If any instrument in payment, by any commercially acceptable means, of any amount”, and (2) by striking “such check” each place it appears and inserting “such instrument”.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that changing the definition of payment instruments affects how the public interacts with the IRS, thus involving participation. However, this is merely a technical amendment to the definition of valid payment methods for tax liabilities. It does not create a process for the public to consult with, advise, or participate in a federal decision-making process. It is a substantive rule change, not a participatory mechanism.
